I have already spoken on the percentage of reduction on stock, and I wish to say a few words with regard to the revaluation of land. The general principle governing that question has been so well stated by hon. members who have preceded me, notably the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) and the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) that I will not go into that phase of it, except to give a general support to their views. I wish, however, to deal with a matter which they did not cover, and that is a phase of this land question as it arises in British Columbia. As we know, the prairie is comparatively easy farming. In British Columbia, with very few exceptions, it is a question of going into the bush, and as the expression goes, hewing out a home. It sounds very nice and romantic, but it really should be interpreted, grubbing up stumps. The district I more particularly wish to allude to is the settlement in the neighbourhood of Courtenay and Merville. The provincial government undertook to make a settlement there very soon after the return of the men. They undertook to clear so many acres for each man, and the cost ran from $400 to $450 an acre, exclusive of the price of the land, and it was not very well cleared even then. The situation became so acute that the provincial government were compelled, by the force of circumstances and by the fact that the men were utterly incapable of carrying on under the burden which that high cost of clearing imposed upon them, to make a revaluation of the land by which they cut the value down substantially. The Dominion farms lie right alongside that district, and the land and stumps are similar. When the Prime Minister and his party were in British Columbia last summer they gave us the honour of a visit in the Courtenay district, and the Prime Minister was kind enough to receive a deputation of soldier settlers, and also went out and I think the Minister without portfolio, from Ottawa, went with him to see the land. We showed them land with stumps which would run from two and a half to four feet in diameter, and some even five feet. They were so close together in places that you could very nearly walk across the land without treading on the soil. This land was adjacent to Merville. It will take nearly a box of powder to blow out one stump, and the powder will cost about nine dollars and the labour in addition. It will occupy a space of from ten to fifteen square yards. When you have got it out you have a large hole in the ground, and when you have filled it in, then you have a piece of land that will not grow anything for from two to five years, because the sub-soil has been brought to the surface. Until it has the aeration of the air and sun on it, it will not grow anything. That is the sort of land we showed the Prime Minister. If you estimate the stumps from thirty to forty to an acre on the basis I have suggested, it wall cost from $300 to' $400 an acre to clear this land after you have bought it. It is not like prairie land that you can put a plough right into.
Is this land within the district that was so eloquently described yesterday by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King) as being highly productive?
That is worse still.

The district which the minister was describing yesterday has no connection with this. But if my hon. friend wishes to go into that side line, I may say that the Comox valley is known as the garden of British Columbia, delta lands formed many years ago by rivers and they are covered with a deep loam. What I am describing is bush lands covered by heavy timber, and all British Columbians know that this land is second class land even after it has been ex-
Soldier Settlement Act

pensively cleared in the way I have indicated. This delegation that waited on the Prime Minister showed that they paid $45 an acre for that land in its uncleared state. They also showed that the present price of land in a similar condition right alongside was $7.50 an acre. Further than that, they showed that the value of that wild land at the time they bought it was only $7.50 an acre and they are prepared to produce evidence to that effect. It is frankly admitted there was bad management in the purchase of it.
I think the late government and the present government are to be congratulated on the almost entire freedom from any suggestion of graft in the purchase of all these lands. That was a wonderful achievement. It was a big order. There was no experience to guide those who handled the matter, and yet there have been few suggestions of any impropriety in the purchase. The trouble has occurred more in the shape of bad judgment. Men not fit for their jobs got appointed as supervisors and they lent themselves to the purchase of land at too high a price. There was also what I might almost call an . hysterical condition prevailing at the time. There was a great condition of emergency. These men were coming home by the thousands and something had to be done for them. They were exigent in their demands, and that attitude was more or less reflected in the action of the government. Be that as it may, these lands were bought at $45 an acre when they were never worth even at that time more than $7.50 an acre, according to the public Valuation. I have an intimate acquaintance with this class of land, because many yearn ago I took up a quarter section of land of the same character, though not nearly as heavily wooded. I paid $3 an acre for it, just three hundred times too much, because anyone who clears land of that description ought to get it for nothing and be given a bonus for clearing it. I speak from painful and practical experience in the matter.
The minister tells us that there is no need to revalue this land; that where they have salvaged1 lands, they have resold them at a better price. Naturally, if you have a lot of stuff on your hands, whether it is farms or horses or anything else, you sell the best first, because the public will always buy the best first and you cannot make a comparison by taking the picked pieces1 which are sold first. When it is all sold-and it will, be difficult to sell a great deal of it-they will have an idea whether they can salvage it at a better price than they paid for it, and I am satisfied that that will not be the case.
	*
I have looked up the minister's remarks in Hansard, and he said that while he did not admit there was any need for revaluation and he was not prepared to admit that the value of lands had fallen since these men bought their farms, he did admit that in certain cases they had been, I think he said, overpurchased. If that is the case, we will accept it for the moment for the sake of argument, although I cannot accept it from my own experience. We will say it is true that in the great majority of cases the land has not gone down in value. If that is the case, how much easier it is to pass this legislation for which we are asking? In the cases where he does admit there was overpurchase or impropriety or graft, how much more necessary and easier it will be for us to remedy those particular and, as he suggests, more or less isolated) cases. This will make it easy to put the matter right at a comparatively low expenditure. Another suggestion is made that if we go into this it will be too costly. The reasons I have already given would operate against that. If there are not many cases, it will not be costly. But another reason is that it cannot be costing you anything if it is already lost. The value of these properties disappeared six years ago, or whatever the period was when the government supervisors recommended) 'the purchase of the '.land at $45 an acre when it was worth then only $7.50 and is worth only that now. To legislate out a bad debt will not make you any poorer. It is simply a question of paper bookkeeping and of not throwing out men who are now on the land. The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) said: Is it not right and proper that the Soldier Settlement Board should deal with this matter as a business enterprise? By all means, and if you have an insolvent debtor on your hands, is it not good business methods to make the best you can out of your loss, not to increase it, not to stand by and say: We will demand our pound of flesh, when you know perfectly well it is unobtainable? Nothing can be gained by that. Is it not better to help the debtor if possible so as to retrieve as much as you can reasonably, and let the rest go rather than insist on your pound of flesh and, perhaps, in the long run get a great deal less? There is additional encouragement in this case in that we would be keeping the soldier on the land. Surely that is desirable. He has put his money and so on into dt. If we salvage him, which is a polite way of throwing him out, and sell the land to someone else who is not a soldier, who may be a British subject, but

Soldier Settlement Act
who was not a soldier for us, that man will not pay more than the standard value. He will take care to see that he does not pay any more than the actual cash value to-day. What is to be gained by throwing out this soldier who, after all, has some claims, because when he came back from the war he was not familiar with real estate values and with the locality. We sat at home; we knew the values and how to sell to the best advantage. But these men were, perhaps, not locally informed as much as they might be. They came at any rate and located, and it is in our interest, apart from any sentimental regard at all, to see that they stay on the land if that is reasonably possible, vhich will involve no real loss to the general public funds, because you are not going to get the full price out of them in any case. You can force them out if you like and that is all you will do.
As regards the forty per cent and the twenty per cent on stock, I have already dealt with that. While I regret very much to see it, possibly that will be regarded by the men as a half measure that is better than nothing. But this is such a far more important issue that I would beseech the government to reconsider it. I do not think there was an absolute note of finality in the minister's remarks, and I believe if this committee showed a full expression of its views on the matter, he might yet be led to reconsider the question of revaluation. It is of no use to talk about revaluing the land twenty-five years from now. You might as well talk about revaluing it in, the next world. These men will be gone. They cannot wait for twenty-five years paying interest on an absurd valuation with some vague, nebulous hope that twenty-five years from now they may have the land revalued. That is not business. If you are going to give the man relief, give it to him now and let him know exactly what he has to face. In that event he will be encouraged to go ahead. Men who are now hanging fire will say: This is something we can overtake, and they will make an endeavour to meet their obligations if they are brought down to a reasonable basis. I hope the minister will be induced to reconsider this phase of the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Is that the
only case in the hon. member's constituency or on the island in which there has been an overvaluation? A valuation of $45 would seem to be enormous when the actual value of the land was $7.50. Surely there are not many cases of that kind.

The deputation that met the Prime Minister and his party consisted of only three or four, but if I remember rightly their association numbered something like forty, although I am speaking only from memory. I have no doubt there were other cases, but this particular settlement would be somewhere about that number.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is not generally true of the soldier settlers.

I speak only of that particular place but I know other places in my district where the same thing is moTe or less true, such as down in the lower portion, in the neighbourhood of Errington and Parks-ville; and in a general way the same thing is true of every section of land where these men were put on what is known as high bush-lands, where the removal of the stumps would cost anywhere from $200 to $400 an acre. And it is well known that after this has been done the land is only what we would call second class; you could not grow roots with any great success. The land is dry and you have to put your crop in early in the season, hoping to take it out before the dTy weather comes. The crop would be limited to oats hay, timothy and produce of that kind.

I had not the advantage of hearing the discussion this afternoon of this important and long anticipated resolution. I must express regret that the government in the resolution which they have proposed have not adopted the percentage revaluation of live stock which, if I remember rightly, was agreed to by the special parliamentary committee of last year. The percentages had been worked out by that committee with great care, after hearing all the officials from the department, and the proposal was that 60 per cent and 40 per cent would afford reasonable reductions. I join with others who have spoken in regretting that the government has not provided for this 60 per cent and 40 per cent revaluation; and I agree with the hon. member (Mr. Neill) that a far more important matter than the one we have under consideration is the matter which the government has apparently omitted, namely, revaluation of soldier land.
I have not been able in the limited time at my disposal to place my finger on the exact spot in the evidence of last year, but I know that that evidence indicated that some 4,500 soldiers had become adjustment cases, having abandoned the land, and the department was left with the live stock as well as the land of these abandoning settlers. In addition to that, as I believe the evidence will show,
Soldier Settlement Act

about 5,000 more soldiers are as it were shivering on the brink. A favourable turn in the tide of fortune would give these men an opportunity to prosper, whereas a recurrence of the conditions' which have persisted through all these latter years will simply result in their cases also passing into the adjustment class. Their farms will be salvaged while those that are not salvaged will perhaps be abandoned because of failure or inability on the part of the soldiers to caTry on successfully.
It is with regard to these 5,000 soldiers that parliament must take some effective action. These men must if possible be preserved on the land, because if these farms revert to the government there can be no question that the government will lose a very large amount of money, a larger amount than would be lost by any revaluation that might be made. It is suggested that a system of revaluation would be altogether too . costly, but it is my view that failure to undertake a revaluation will be much more costly. This was a tremendous colonization scheme which the Dominion adopted, and it seems to me that the government can very well take every possible step to ensure its success. If they do not then they will have more abandoned land on their hands and the soldiers will have to go to other countries to find more favourable opportunities to achieve success. And apart from all that the country will be burdened with a tremendous loss.
Last year this situation was thoroughly considered and the committee had before it two possible steps that might be taken. In the first place there was suggested what might be called mass action; it was proposed to give a remission of interest to every soldier irrespective of whether or not he was successful. It was suggested that the benefits of such interest remission should be shared alike by the deserving and the undeserving. Frankly, I do not approve of that method of handling the situation; it would be only a temporary measure at best and could not be successful. In 1922 the system of interest remission was tried and at that time, although I am not a farmer, I expressed the fear that such a plan would not succeed; and certainly the intervening years have amply demonstrated the correctness of the view I then took. I would point out that this scheme of interest remission is not fair either to the soldiers or to the public at large. It is not fair that the soldier who does not need it should get it, nor is it fair that the public should be called upon to bear the burden of a reduction in interest which is unnecessary

and which advantages many of the undeserving as well as the deserving. The other method of handling the matter is by a system of revaluation of the land-individual action with respect to every parcel of land, having in mind the applicant himself, his efforts in the past, the possibilities of his success in the future, and the probable conditions for the future. Taking all these things into consideration, somebody could determine whether or not a revaluation in any particular case should be undertaken. I believe that a revaluation of the land should be carried out by a competent organized arbitration board in each land settlement district. I do not for a moment suggest any cumbersome machinery; but if the Soldier Settlement Board cannot make an effective and final arrangement with the soldiers themselves, then a simple arbitration board should be constituted *which would make a final award so far as reduction in the capital value of the land is concerned.
I regret that the minister proposes no action in this regard, for I certainly think that action is called for. I had understood all along that something was to be done, and I am quite sure that a large number of soldiers are vitally interested in the proposition. When therefore they hear the minister's decree in this matter they will regard it as to some extent the death knell of their hopes, and a great many of them will join the long list of those who have already abandoned the land. In conclusion, I say that Canada cannot afford now to fail to undertake this task. If we do not undertake it to-day we are bound to undertake it to-morrow; and before we have further tremendous losses on our hands why should we not discharge today the duty which lies before us? I have no doubt that if the government will reconsider this matter carefully they will find that in instituting some system of land revaluation at this session they would merit the confidence and esteem of returned soldiers generally.

Mr. Chairman, I never
want to let an opportunity go by to urge on parliament the necessity of doing something this session to relieve our returned men. A great many of them in my constituency are making a desperate effort to hold on until they know what is going to be done this session to help them out. They qre up against an impossibility, as we all know, because their land has doubled in value since they bought it; but not in dollars and cents; in this respect its value perhaps has not varied very much; but the value of the products

Soldier Settlement Act
they get off that land has been cut in two, and that virtually means doubling the price of their land. And all of the trouble does not lie there even. The cost of the stock and equipment and the land taken together makes their position absolutely untenable. I have discussed with a good many of them how much they thought would have to be cut off from their indebtedness before they would have the courage to carry on until they made good, and their estimate varies all the way from 30 to 50 per cent. I think we can strike between those two marks and get approximately the right percentage. I think most of them are looking to the Ralston commission's report as a guide for parliament, and they would probably be satisfied if its recommendations were carried into effect. I have often wondered whether it would not perhaps be better to cut a certain percentage off each man's indebtedness on his undertaking to carry on and try to make good if this measure of relief is given. I think that would suit the men just as well as a revaluation. In fact I do not know what we could do that would relieve them by revaluing their land on the basis of dollars and cents, because their ability to pay depends on what they can obtain from the produce of their land, and such a revaluation might not be altogether satisfactory as well as being difficult and expensive to carry out. I am so convinced that these men should be kept on the land if it is at all possible that I want to urge on the House that something should be done this session to that end, for if we wait even until another session many of these men will have become discouraged and drift into the towns, where they will be hun'ing for jobs that other people already need very badly, and we cannot afford to have that condition of affairs take place in connection with the returned men. The country is going to lose a certain amount of money, but I do not think we need be so afraid of losing a few dollars, because these men have already lost more than we can repay them in a lifetime. We want to do something that will keep them on the land, for they are better settlers than any other men we may replace them with. These soldier settlers may not all make good, but where will you find any class of people who are uniformly successful? As one hon. member said this afternoon, when these soldier settlers went on the land even men of the soberest and soundest judgment had wild ideas of what could be done, and many of them expanded their business and lost heavily. So we should not blame the soldier settlers if under the advice of the board some of them have 228
made mistakes. Under any circumstances I do not think we can afford to let this session close without doing something to relieve these men so that they may know where they are at. As I said before, I think the better plan would be to cut a certain percentage off each man's indebtedness.-

Would not a flat reduction
in each man's case result in a great many men getting a small reduction who do not want it and are not entitled to it, while those who are badly in need of help would get a very small reduction which would be no real value to them?

Very likely some inequalities would crop up, but I think it would be a fairer way than attempting a revaluation and would be less expensive. As we all know, taxation involves a certain amount of inequality, and we cannot get these matters on an absolutely accurate basis and this is a very similar problem. Many of the men have tried to carry on and they have kept reports from day to day of what they have done. I have looked over some of them and I think they would be a credit to any business man. Most of these reports disclose heavy losses, and unless something is done it is certain that many of the men will lose their own money as well as their soldier settlement money. It is vitally important that we act at once, and I would warn the House of the danger of delay. Twenty-five years from now there will never be any need of a revaluation, because long before that time many of these men will have been forced to give up what already appears to them to be a well-nigh hopeless struggle. I am a practical farmer, and I think I know what they are up against, and if I were in their place I believe I would be just as much discouraged as they are. I like to see young people brought up to understand the necesssity of laying the foundation for a competence that will take care of them in their old age, but if they drift along beyond a certain point they lose the inclination to make the necessary effort to establish themselves on a firm basis. While I am very anxious to see everybody do what he can to take care of himself, I cannot help thinking that the position of these men when they took up land was different from that of the ordinary citizen. It is either a case of their making good or of their becoming a charge on the country. The matter is a serious one, and the appeal on behalf of the men is such that if the hearts of hon. members of the House are right, something will be done this session if at all possible.

Soldier Settlement Act

I cannot retain my
seat in silence and thereby intimate that I am satisfied with this legislation. I feel that the government are not doing enough in this legislation for the soldier settlers. In my constituency there are quite a number of these settlers, and I have the highest admiration for the manner in which they have conducted themselves, for the work they have done and for their efforts to make good in the face of an almost impossible situation. I am confident that the great majority of them have done the best they could with the properties they have taken hold of, but they have had much to contend with. The class of farming done in New Westminster constituency is more or less mixed farming. After the soldier settlers had taken over their properties certain changes were made in the United States tariff, and those changes have had a very material effect on the soldier settlers. We produce in the Fraser valley such commodities as hay, fruit, potatoes, butter, cheese, eggs, cattle. We find that the United States tariff on hay is $4 a ton, while the Canadian tariff is $2; on fruits, United States, 35 per cent; Canada, 25 per cent.

As to the expediency
of passing the legislation, yes.

I think the government should consider this question of the revaluation of the lands. There is no doubt that in my constituency as well as in others, lands were valued at too high a figure; that a revaluation either by a commission or by the department would show that the soldiers paid altogether too much for their land. I join with other

hon. members in demanding that the government should at this session make some provision for a scientific revaluation of these lands. I understood the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) to say that he was not in favour of interest remission. I do not agree with him in that; I think it is a matter which might well be considered. There is a very strong feeling in my constituency among those interested in the soldier settlers, as well as among the soldier settlers themselves, that this would be an effective way of showing consideration to these men. The hon. member who preceded me mentioned the matter of debt reduction. That is another method which might be considered. The hon. member for Comox-Albemi suggested that some men might get reductions who did not want them, but it seems to me that that would be contrary to human nature, because any soldier settler or anybody else would want whatever consideration he could get in that line.

And are the soldier
settlers not entitled to all the reduction they
can get?

I think they are; I
quite agree with the hon. member. We should treat these men fairly. It should not be a case of a money lender demanding his pound of flesh. The department, I know, has been anxious to get back all the money it can; in fact some of the representatives of the government, I think, have been rather hard on the men, and there have been cases where the men have been badly treated. But there is something more to consider than the business proposition of getting back the money which has been loaned. The original idea of settling soldiers on our lands was a splendid one. It is all right to expect them to pay if they can, but I would urge on the government the necessity of doing something more than is contemplated in this legislation.

I would like to add my voice to the appeal made to the government for a more generous measure regarding the revaluation of the soldiers' live stock and land. Some time ago I received a letter from the provincial secretary of the Great War Veterans' Association giving an account of a convention that was held at Saskatoon on the 17th, ISth, and 19th of March. If there is one thing noticeable about the resolutions that were passed at that convention, it is their reasonableness and the moderate tone in which the convention put forth their demands.

Soldier Settlement Act
Regarding land revaluation the resolution
reads:
Whereas the price agreed to be paid by soldier settlers for land bought from the Soldiers' Settlement Board is too high in most cases and is a burden which will be impossible to carry and unless adjusted will result in the abandoning of the land, the failure of the scheme, the loss of the settler's stake and hardship and suffering,
Therefore be it resolved (a) that the Soldier Settlement Act be so amended as to make provision for the revaluation of all land (particularly raw crown land) purchased by soldier settlers from the Soldiers' Settlement Board, such valuation to be on an arbitration basis, to be optional with the settler and to be based on the condition of the land at the time of purchase, and that the necessary adjustments be made accordingly. (b) That there be a revaluation board in each district consisting of three members, one to be appointed by the Great War Veterans' Association, one to be the District Superintendent, the third to be a disinterested man familiar with land values to be appointed by the two already appointed.
That is moderate in tone, and I think very reasonable. Their resolution regarding the revaluation of stock is based on what we took to be the promise of the government twelve months ago, and reads as follows:
That the act be further amended so that a capital cut be made in the price of stock purchased from the board as follows:
60 per cent reduction of the purchase price where stock purchased prior to December 31, 1920.
40 per cent reduction of the purchase price whore stock purchased prior to December 31, 1921.
20 per cent reduction of the purchase price where stock purchased prior to December 31, 1922.
Speaking as a practical farmer I must say that during the period in which the soldiers have been settled on the land, it has been practically impossible to make ends meet. Between drought and the deflation of prices even the experienced settler could hardly make good. I think the soldier settler who has failed to make good on the land since 1918 certainly has a claim on this country. He was expected to be looked after, I know, but most of these men are very self-reliant, and I do know many cases where hardship has existed on the farms both among the men and the women during the last two or three winters. I say they are deserving of all the help we can give them. They have a claim on the country. Once a. man has faced death for the defence of his own home and of his fellow countrymen he must not be left in a precarious position during the rest of his days; I think it is only reasonable to take that stand.
While it is plain to this House that the members, particularly on this side, are united in their appeal to the government for a more generous measure of revaluation, if the government want a more pronounced verdict from our own group I would ask them to lay this 228i
over for the present as a great many of our members are away to-day attending the funeral of the late Mr. Drummond. I think it would be well for the government to reconsider this resolution, which is to be the basis of legislation to follow, and bring in later a more generous measure both as regards live stock and land. I appeal to the government to do this.

Mr. Chairman, I must
confess at the outset that I am very greatly disappointed in the measure that is proposed to be brought before the House with reference to the revaluation of soldiers' stock and equipment. I felt assured last year when the committee's report was adopted by this House, with certain reservations by the Minister of the Interior, that we could not expect anything less than the recommendations of the committee as to the revaluation of the stock at least. I also hoped that there would be a substantial reduction in the liability of the soldier with regard to his land.
I was somewhat surprised this afternoon to hear some of the arguments the Acting Minister of Finance put up in defence of his present stand on this legislation. In the first place he said that the soldier settler was satisfied with the price of the land. I think, Mr. Chairman, those of us who were fairly closely connected with the 9 p.m. work at that time, and everybody in this country as well, realized that these soldiers were young men who had spent three or four years in the zone of war, and knew nothing or very little at all events about prices here at that time. There was a boom on then for greater production, and prices were high. I know that in the province from which I come there is a very great difference in prices to-day from what they were in 1919-1920 when this scheme was brought into effect. At that time our farmers were getting $20 a ton for hay and two or three dollars a barrel for potatoes. Potatoes are to our province what wheat is to the west; it is our big crop for export, and during the present season our farmers received only eight dollars a ton for hay and I think on an average of sixty cents a barrel for potatoes during the whole season, and thousands of barrels will not be marketed at all, but will simply be dumped, because there will be no market for them. In fact, in only one year of the last four years has the potato grower got the actual cost of growing the crop, and that was in the year 1923, when he got a little more than the actual cost of growing. But in the other three years he
Soldier Settlement Act

made a debt on the cost of his production. So conditions are very different to-day from what they were in 1919-1920. Members say that very much higher prices were being paid in Canada then than were justified, but it is not true of New Brunswick. If the price of farm produce had remained' at the level of 1919-1920 the soldiers could have paid for their farms at the price they bought them for, but due to the very great deflation in the price of our crop for export in the last four years the farmers in New Brunswick who had a reserve, who were out of debt, who owned their farms and owed nothing to anybody, have been compelled to use up their reserves. Therefore the soldier settlers have had absolutely no chance to make good, and the amazing part of it to my mind is that a number of them have been able to make payments as they came due. Others have made partial payments.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What is the difference between the general interest rate in New Brunswick as against the five per cent the soldiers get?

I think a man would
have had no difficulty four years ago in getting interest at six per cent on a mortgage.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Are they
getting that to-day?

I do not think so. I
doubt if you could get a mortgage on a farm at all to-day. I was talking to a man on Friday or Saturday last, when I was home over the week end, who told me he had foreclosed two mortgages in the last two years. One was on a splendid farm on which the buildings were insured for $10,000, a good producing farm, with excellent buildings, and within less than half a mile of a railroad. This man had a mortgage of $5,000 on that farm, and when he foreclosed he could not get a bid at all. He had a mortgage on another farm of a little less value, farm possibly worth $10,000. He had a mortgage of $4,000 on that, and he could not get a bid on it, when he foreclosed last spring. Real estate in the shape of farm land is a drug on the market in New Brunswick at the present time.	There are no sales being
made; nobody wants farm land.
Some members have spoken of urging the soldier settlers in their home constituencies to hang on in the hope that the government was going to carry out the recommendations of last year's committee. This has been done in New Brunswick by numbers of men as well as by myself.	A number of the soldier
settlers have been hanging on, with the pretty

firm belief that the government might put into effect the recommendations of last year's committee. I should like to urge the government to at least extend the remission of interest, if they do not wish to make it absolute. Let them extend it for five years or even three years, and thus give these men some hope that eventually they may be able to make good. If times were to revive and became as good as they were in 1920, there might be a possibility of the men paying for the farms.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is not arguing that we should make a general reduction.

There is a possibility
it would not be necessary. Personally I think it would. I was in favour-and the committee were practically unanimously in favour-of either a revaluation or a remission of interest. I think the large majority of the committee were in favour of the remission of interest, because a physical revaluation would entail a good deal of cost that would not come to the soldier settler. It wou^d be eaten up in overhead expenses in making the revaluation. In the case of a remission of interest the loss to the country would all go to the soldier. There would be no overhead in making that reduction. One of the reasons why I was so strongly in favour of this reduction of the capital indebtedness-you may call it remission of interest or revaluation, or whatever you like-was that it would mean a smaller loss to the country than would be entailed if you maintained the present price with the present interest, because it is my candid belief that there will not be fifty per cent of the soldier settlers on the farms in New Brunswick in a few years unless something is done along this line. I think the government realize what failure to give this relief will mean. These people will drift into the cities, to swell the ranks of the unemployed, or, what is possibly worse, they will drift into the United States, as many of our young men are doing, and it will not be due to the want of high protection, as our good friends to the right would lead us to believe, but because farm produce is not selling for what it will cost to grow it. The drift from this country is not from the industrial centres, but from the farm, I am very sorry to say. I live in a county called the garden of New Brunswick from an agricultural point of view. I can stand in my door and count seven vacant farm houses in sight of where I live, and I live in as good a part of the country as can be found. My

Soldier Settlement Act
district is called the garden county of the province and yet our young men are leaving, old folks who cannot afford to hire help at the present price of produce are closing down and going to live with their sons in New Brunswick or in the United States, and the farm houses are being abandoned. It is not an industrial drift from the province, but an exodus from the farms.
Another matter I shall deal with is the report of the Soldier Settlement Board as to the resale of lands for a greater price than they cost. I think this report is very misleading indeed, but I do not want to impute any wrong motives to the Soldier Settlement Board. I think they have been as efficient as it is possible for human beings to be, and have handled the situation as well as could be expected, but the circumstances of the agricultural industry are such that conditions have been brought about over which nobody has any control. I think the report is very misleading. In the first place this supposed surplus price at Which properties are sold over the cost is not really a surplus over cost, it is a surplus over what the government held on the property and did not include the ten per cent paid by the soldier. If that were figured in I think there would be no surplus but a loss.

I think the report made
it clear that it did not include the ten per cent.

I do not think so. I
know it is not clear to the public. We men on the committee know it perfectly well, but to the man on the street it is not clear. When the report was circulated that this land was sold for $700,000 or $800,000 more than it cost-that is the way it was reported in the papers-the man on the street believed that that was actually true. Then these sales, if they were made for cash, would even carry more conviction still; but the fact is that these sales are made on a promise to pay that is possibly not a bit better than the promise the soldier settler made, and just as impossible of being fulfilled. If the board were selling the land for cash the government could well say that they had made a profit on the transaction, but I am afraid they will find eventually that they have made as great a loss on the last sale as was made on the first sale. They will have the lands back on their hands. What will happen if even fifty per cent of the soldier settlers abandon the farms and the lands come back on the government's hands, with the agricultural industry in its present depressed state?
Nobody wants to purchase the land and nobody will want to rent it. I know that in our province farmers to-day individually have more land than they oan work, because it will not pay them to hire help. A man who 'has his own help can make a living if he is not in debt, but he cannot h-ire help at the present prices. The soldier who has moved off the land has lost the ten per cent he paid down on the farm, a matter of four or five or six hundred dollars as the case may be, and he has lost three or four of the best years of his life. He has struggled along under all kinds of hardship and poverty, and at last has been compelled to take his little family and go out on the road without a dollar, hunt for a job, and try to get a house to live in while he earns enough to pay the rent. It is a deplorable picture of the men who marched away from us so gaily ten years ago. I think we all remember the kind of promises that were ringing in their ears when they were told that they and their dependents would be looked after and that they would not have to worry about the future. It is a sorry picture to-day as compared with those promises. This suggestion that the adjustment might be made at the end of twenty-five years is futile, because, as I said, I do not think fifty per cent of the farmer settlers will be on the land at the end of a few years. I have no hesitation in saying that if their present financial obligations are enforced there will be few of them here at the end of ten or fifteen years, and if we are to retain these men the adjustment must be made. While I was very strongly of the opinion last year that the government would be well advised to cut out the repayment of interest entirely, I think if they get the principal back without interest they will suffer a smaller loss than they will sustain it the men abandon the farms.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In view of the statement of my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni this afternoon, the remission of interest will not meet this case?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Nor will it meet the case mentioned by my bon. friend from Dauphin. With all due respect to the statement of my hon. friend from Victoria and Carleton, if I caught the drift of his remarks correctly, he said that the land was purchased reasonably well in New Brunswick-

In view of the then price of farm produce.
Soldier Settlement Act

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Then in
common with all other lands their values must have been on about an equality. The Strongest argument in my -opinion for a -revaluation- and I think perhaps it can hardly be disputed -is the fact that in some -cases lands were purchased -at a price beyond their value.
I think so, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: You cannot cure that by a reduction in interest. I just want the hon. gentleman to get a correct idea of this situation when it -comes to the question of an equitable adjustment of land values. I was rather struck with the suggestion of -the hon. member for Bow River that you -might leave it entirely to the board; but to leave the -matter, as suggested by the hon. member for -Saskatoon, to a local board in each locality -certainly in my opinion would not tend to an equitable readjustment of this situation. I think the discussion this afternoon has brought out many of the difficulties that have to -be met if this -problem is to be solved correctly.

I am not married to
any particular method. In my opinion, unless something is done, you are going to have dissatisfaction amongst the soldier settlers in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon.
member's argument is that there should be a general reduction despite special conditions that may prevail,

I think so. I stated a few minutes ago that a temporary remission of interest will encourage some men to hold on who will not hold on if something is not done. If something is not done, some farmers . in New Brunswick will leave their farms thi3 summer.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Remission
of interest has been given.

Yes, and it has encouraged them. As an hon. member said this afternoon, when the remission of interest was made in 1922 it did encourage the soldiers. Numbers of them hung on in the hope that conditions would -become better. If conditions continue as they are in New Brunswick, it will not matter what is done by the government, because farmers will leave who -do not owe anybody on account of the price of farm produce being so low in comparison with prices of other commodities.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The point
my hon. friend is making is that the soldier is no worse off in New Brunswick than his farmer neighbour.

He is much worse off.
Had the price of farm produce remained as it was in 1920, he would have had a hard struggle. Anyone who has farmed knows that a man who is paying interest on ninety per cent of his whole investment has a tremendous handicap as compared with the man who is out of debt.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
When a man undertakes an obligation of that sort, he has a tremendous handicap in any case.
Mr. -CALDWELL: Yes. I had a very close association with this work because I was on the 'board that helped to -buy the farms in New Brunswick the first year the scheme was put into operation. My view was that -the soldier was taking a big chance. I said:	If
the soldier leaves this farm in ten years, he has paid ten per cent down, he has made some subsequent -payments and the government will make something out of it at -all events. But the soldier is taking all the chances. I did not encourage soldiers to take up this scheme. In fact, I h-ad a -pamphlet printed setting forth to the men who applied to us for loans to buy farms in New Brunswick, just what their obligations and their chances of -making good were. Many of them backed up when they realized the whole situation. Last year the committee of which I was a member recommended that the Soldier Settlement Board have authority to resettle men, to remove them from lands that were not suitable for settlers. I think the board might well be given quite wide powers in special cases such as those cited by the -hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) and in other parts of Canada as well. A portion of Manitoba was cited this afternoon as -being an impossible situation-. These settlers should be moved out of those places if there is an opportunity of settling them on land where they can make good. Last year when this matter was before the committee, I discussed it with a field supervisor in New Brunswick, a man in whose judgment I have unbounded confidence, an excellent man who has seen services overseas and who has made good as field supervisor, and he said that he thought the only possible way to retain these men on the land in New Brunswick was to cut down their capital liability. He agreed that a remission of interest was the simplest, most direct, and least costly way, and that the soldier would get the whole good of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That would be quite all right for New Brunswick on the hon. member's own statement inasmuch as he says that the land was well -bought.

I think it was.

Soldier Settlement Act

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
How would
the thing work out in the case described by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward)?

I would hesitate to set
down any hard and fast rule for the whole of Canada. The board should be given wide powers of discretion in cases of special conditions.
The present proposal is to grant relief only to those who are now on the land and who have not made their payments. The man who had some funds of his own and has made those payments out of those funds, or in some cases the man who has married a wife with money who has put her money into the land, will eventually lose it. The man who has made his payments under this scheme is to be penalized or, at least, he is to derive no benefit under this revaluation of stock. I do not think that is fair. The legislation is not well considered along that line. For instance, the man who has not made any effort will get a benefit out of this. It is doubtful, of course, if it will do him much good either.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The proposal of the committee was along that line, that all should participate just as in the remission of interest.

There is one other
feature which does not come under this legislation, but I should like to speak of it if I might. I refer to taxes on salvaged lands of settlers. I have urged repeatedly on the government in private and public that they should pay the taxes on soldier settler lands that have been salvaged. The argument has been put forward that government land is not taxable. As regards wild lands, that is all right. But when the government comes into territory that is organized into school districts and buys up one-third of the lands, and they become salvaged, it is impossible for the rest of the ratepayers to carry on and educate their children. This is creating an impossible condition in large areas in New Brunswick at the present time, and the government might very well consider the question of paying taxes on these lands.
I want to endorse the suggestion made by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans). Due to the fact that quite a large delegation of the western Progressives have not returned from the Maritimes, and that another quite large delegation are away at a funeral of one of their colleagues, I think the government would be well advised to ask the committee to rise and report progress without
even passing this resolution because a bill will be based on it. The government might well consider the question of bringing down a more generous measure. I would ask them not to pass this resolution to-night, but to allow the committee to rise and report progress and to give the matter further consideration.

Just before six o'clock I
made a few remarks in which I intimated that certain lands purchased for soldiers in Manitoba, had been bought at an excessive price.
I stated that I had information and proof to that effect. I have at hand many documents that would prove that statement, but I do not intend taking up the time of the committee in reading many of them. I will read just two. This was a survey made by Mr. J. H. Martinson, of Douglas, Manitoba. He sent out a circular letter to different bankers and prominent farmers in Canada, men who would know local conditions in these districts, asking them for their opinion about lands purchased by the Soldier Settlement Board. This is a reply by Mr. J. P. Hemier, Manager of the Royal Bank of Canada at Ste. Rose du Lac, Manitoba:
In reply to your letter of the 22nd instant, we would say that land bought for $4,000 in 1919 and 1920 is worth about fifty per cent of that now.
In additional evidence, I will read a communication which Mr. Martinson received from General Hugh Dyer, of Minnedosa. He says, in part:
I yield to no one in my interest in the establishment of returned men on the farm, and speaking generally they have paid 33 per cent too much for everything.
This, I think, will substantiate the statement I made that soldier settlers in my province have paid too much for the land. The minister, this afternoon, intimated-at least that is the- way I understood his remarks -that there had not been so many abandonments. I believe that the hon. member (Mr. Caldwell) made the statement that so far as New Brunswick was concerned he did not think that the abandonments had been excessive owing to the fact that perhaps the soldiers had not been overcharged for the land.

I do not want to be
misunderstood. What I said was that if prices had been maintained at the level they had reached in 1920 the soldiers could have paid for the land at the price at which they had bought it. In other words, I do not think that the price was excessive at the time they bought the land.
Soldier Settlement Act

Well, had wheat remained at $2.50 per bushel in western Canada the returned men in that part of the country would also have been able to pay for the land. But unfortunately that is not the case. Now, I have an abundance of material to show the present intolerable position of the returned men. Mr. G. W. Langdon, the reeve of Lake-view municipality of Manitoba, made investigations among the different municipalities of the province to discover how many farms had been abandoned in each municipality. He submitted to each municipality certain questions to which he received replies, and while I will not read them all, there are one or two which I should like to quote. The first municipality in regard to which figures are given is McCreary:
1.	How many soldier settlers located in your municipality? 80.
2.	How may quarter sections did they secure? 85.
3.	How many soldiers have to date abandoned their lands? 41.
This would be over 50 per cent. The next information concerns the municipality of Eriksdale:
1.	How many soldier settlers located in your municipality ? 160.
2.	How many quarter sections did they secure? 175.
3.	How many soldiers have to date abandoned their lands? 135.
In this case the abandonments are more than 70 per cent. Next I take the municipality of Westbourne in my own constituency:
1.	How many soldier settlers located in your municipality? 57.
2.	How many quarter sections did they secure? 63.
3.	How many soldiers have to date abandoned their lands? 23.
That would be almost 50 per cent, I think that the municipality that has been affected to the greatest extent is that of Mr. Langdon himself. These are all statutory declarations that can be vouched for, and this is the information in regard to Lakeview:
1.	How many soldiers located in your municipality? 100.
2.	How many quarter sections did they secure? 151.
3.	How many soldiers have to date abandoned their lands? 61.
4.	How many of these were not former residents of your municipality? 49.
5.	How many quarter sections thus abandoned? 91.
6.	Approximate amount of your taxes lost through abandonments? $12,037.
7.	Amount of outstanding taxes on non-abandoned Soldier Settlement lands? $9,615.
Now, in addition to losing the taxes on these lands the municipality had to make good between $1,000 and $2,000 on account of hospital expenses incurred by the returned men who had no funds with which to pay their bills.

I was speaking about the soldiers who had abandoned their lands, and was referring to the necessity for a revaluation, not only of stock and equipment but of the lands themselves as well. I am fully in sympathy with the resolution before the House but I do not think it goes far enough and I hope the government will reconsider it and take into consideration the advisability of putting into effect some system of revaluing the lands of soldier settlers. I want to offer a word for the returned men who are carrying on, clinging to their farms in the hope of making both ends meet and of eking out an existence for themselves and their families. This matter was referred to by the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton, who pointed out that lands abandoned and reverting to the crown became non-taxable. This is a deplorable situation in the municipalities such as I have mentioned, like Lakeview. Hon. members know that settlers coming into a new district have to open new roads, build schools, and establish other necessary institutions. All these things were done, and the soldiers have now abandoned the land to the extent, of some 60 per cent. All that abandoned land which has now reverted to the crown is exempt from taxation, notwithstanding that the maintenance of all the roads, the schools and so forth must be shouldered by the remaining soldiers and the other settlers in those districts. This entails a considerable hardship on the residents that are now there, and it will spell further abandonments if the government do not reconsider their policy and have these abandoned lands which have reverted to the Dominion taxed as they were before. I believe the government is taking the attitude that it will allow these lands to be taxed provided the provincial governments will undertake to do the same so far as provincial lands are concerned. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Argenteuil) is now here and I should like him to answer this question: Will the Dominion government undertake to have these lands taxed if the provincial governments will agree to the taxation for municipal purposes of provincial lands?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There was a delegation from the organized municipalities of Alberta and Saskatchewan, and as hon. gentlemen no doubt know, this matter has been before parliament annually. One of the difficulties in regard to the taxation of these lands that have reverted to the crown would be that such taxation would open the door to the taxation of all crown lands. I can

Soldier Settlement Act
only express my own opinion on this matter inasmuch as the subject has not been discussed by the government since the delegation made their representation; but it would seem to me that where land which was formerly owned privately in the municipality was purchased by the board and has now been abandoned, becoming crown land, perhaps some consideration might be given. On the other hand, however, there is so much of this area which was crown land previously and was not taxed prior to the time the soldiers went on it that some distinction would have to be made.

Does not the minister
think that in view of the fact that the government purchased the land and put soldiers upon it, the land in that way becoming organized into school districts, it should be liable for taxation? What will happen to the people who are left?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am not
familiar with the conditions in the east, but in the west one or two million acres of land went into this arrangement which undoubtedly might have been settled but which, until patented, certainly would not be liable for taxation.
That does not apply to New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I say therefore that a distinction must be drawn between the two classes of land.

Does the minister say now that lands that were on the tax roll prior to the Soldier Settlement Board purchasing them should in his opinion be liable for taxation now, even though they have reverted to the crown?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I want to
be perfectly clear on this question. Hansard has a habit of taking down exactly what is said, and sometimes a meaning is attributed to words other than that which is intended. I want it to be perfectly well understood that this matter has not been discussed by the government, but that so far as I am concerned I think that possibly there is some claim. So far, however, the government has not discussed the point at all and no decision has been arrived at.

I am glad that the minister shows some sympathy in this regard. There is no doubt that it is eminently unfair that lands which formerly were taxed for municipal purposes and were then sold to soldier settlers, and which are now abandoned,
reverting to the government, should be allowed to go without taxation. After the municipalities have built roads and maintained all the other institutions that go to make up a community, it is unfair that they should be obliged to continue the maintenance of these things while these abandoned lands are untaxed. So far as the municipality of Lakeview is concerned, they have decided to tax all the lands that are rented to the incoming settlers. I have before me a letter in which the complaint is made that the reeve of the municipality had driven out certain settlers who had gone in. The Soldier Settlement Board had gone to the trouble of bringing in new settlers, and when they found out that the municipality expected them to pay taxes they abandoned the land again. It seems to me very unfair to expect any municipality to carry these or any other settlers tax free, and I think the Soldier Settlement Board should come to the rescue and see that the men they put on these lands will be prepared to pay the local taxes.

Mr. Chairman, the ground has already been pretty fully covered, and I do not expect to be able to add anything new to the discussion, but I should like to focus all the goodwill that has been expressed towards our soldier settlers into some definite action. I must confess that it is difficult to know just how we can get action unless the government will offer to reconsider the whole matter. This has been urged by a number of members, and I wish to 'add1 my voice to 'theirs. I think only one bon. member expressed1 the view that the work undertaken for the returned soldiers by the preceding government was a mistake. I believe that the idea itself was a good one. However, in my 'opinion there was an error in its execution in that the land was not conscripted from the large land1 companies of Canada. Of course, I do not blame the preceding government for not then taking this course, neither do I blame the present government for not adopting it now, because the people of Canada generally are not yet prepared for such action, and even the soldiers themselves who are now abandoning their land, being unable to pay their .taxes much less their interest and capital payments, would no doubt be very much opposed even now to conscription of land. Consequently we have to deal with the situation as it is. I believe the preceding government purchased the land at what was the best possible price under the circumstances. It must not be forgotten that conditions at the time of purchase were abnormal, and prices were just as abnormal as conditions. No one can justly blame either
Soldier Settlement Act

this government or its predecessors in so far as the efficiency of the scheme is concerned. I think the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) put the matter in a nutshell when he pointed >ouit that the land at that time wa3 valued not upon the value of what could be produced upon it, but rather upon an inflated basis; but, he added, if the soldier settlers are ever to pay for their land, they can only do so by what they raise on it in crops. No one so far has denied that it is impossible for them at present prices to raise sufficient crops to meet the instalments of principal and interest on the inflated value which prevailed at the time of purchase. Roughly speaking, I believe the situation is something like this: one-third of the soldier settlers have been able to make their payments regularly; another third may possibly be able to make their payments in the future if they have good luck, or good crops; and the remaining third will ultimately have to abandon itheir land.
Now, the resolution that is before the House, I am sure is, so far as it goes, welcomed by all hon. members, 'but, as has been pointed out, it is not adequate, it does not go far enough even in the revaluation of Stock. It has been urged, and well urged, by a number of hon. gentlemen that the revaluation of land should also be included in this scheme. I do not know how to get the government to assure the House that they will reconsider the situation and undertake to revalue the land on some basis. Of course, I appreciate that to undertake revaluation is a very difficult task, neither would I be expectant that any government could do it perfectly; no doubt there would be some mistakes; but that does not excuse the government from making an attempt to deal with the difficulty. The last government introduced the scheme, imade the purchases of land, provided the money for 't)he soldier settlers, and carried out the whole undertaking to its present stage in a very efficient manner. It is now the task of their, successors to make a slight accommodation which the general deflation has made necessary. That readjustment is imperative if the scheme is to be completely successful.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in order to focus the sentiment that has been so well expressed by many hon. members on some definite point of action, I am going to move an amendment to the resolution. I would not be at all surprised if in a few minutes this amendment is ruled out of order, but I would rather my effort met this fate than be impotent in suggesting a remedy. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland):

That this resolution be amended by adding to it the following words:
That in the opinon of this committee the provisions of this resolution do not adequately meet the requirements of our soldier settlers, and therefore the committee recommends that the government should increase the stock revaluation to sixty per cent and forty per cent respectively, and that a measure of land revaluation is also essential.

Mr. Chairman, at
the very outset of the discussion on this resolution I asked the minister a question, but although he made a very lengthy and informative statement to the committee, he failed to answer my question then or in the course of other statements that he made subsequently. I asked him what he proposed to do for the man who has paid up his indebtedness. Under the terms of this resolution it is proposed1 that:
-in the case of any settler who has not repaid his indebtedness to the board, or who has not abandoned his land, or whose agreement with the board has not been terminated or rescinded, the board shall credit his account with an amount, in reduction of his indebtedness to the board, determined as follows:-
Forty per centum of the purchase price of all live stock advanced to the settler and purchased prior to the first day of October, 1920;
Twenty per centum of the purchase price of all live stock advanced to the settler and purchased on or after the first day of October, 1920, and prior to the first day of October, 1921; and
The settler's account shall be credited with the total amount, determined as aforesaid.
I submit that the soldier settler who has paid up, who has kept his agreement and met his indebtedness by hard work, in many cases even by privation, should get the same generous treatment as those who have not yet paid up. If those who have not paid up are

Soldier Settlement Act
to get credit, the man who has paid up, I submit, should get a rebate, and a resolution which omits to take care of the man who has paid up is an unfair discrimination against him. This resolution anticipates legis-. lation which is a measure of relief, and so far as it goes in that direction it has my support. But considering the people it is designed to relieve, and considering the duty this country owes to those people, the proposed legislation is inadequate, insufficient and niggardly. When th6 men whom it affects were called by their country, they did not hesitate. They did not haggle over percentage; they went, and they gave a hundred per cent. Our treatment of them now should be of the same order. WThen the call comes again, which it. probably will whether we want it to come or not, and whether we are prepared or not

and the less prepared we are the worse it will be for us-I think the Canadian people will do exactly as they did before, that is, any Canadian with a drop of red blood in his veins will do so. But I hope that when the time comes the government of that day will see to it that the willing ones are not left alone to man the first line of defence. I hope that the government of the day, to borrow the words of the hon. member for Bow River, will see to it that every citizen and that all money and all industries and all property are made to do their duty. But that is by the way, perhaps, in discussing this resolution. It has been said by some hon. members that this government and its predecessors have been generous in their treatment of the returned soldier. While they may be so, they have not been too generous. Indeed, they could not be too generous. What they have done for the returned soldiers has been done with public money, not with the private money of any government, and what they have done has been with the consent of and to meet the wishes of the taxpayers of this country, who are the people who pay the bills. Now, the subject that is dealt with by this resolution was referred to a special committee well qualified to consider the matter and to advise the House, and after very careful and complete consideration it made certain recommendations. There was every expectation that the government would respond to these recommendations and do what it could to carry them out. Among other things the committee recommended that a 60 per cent and a 40 per cent rebate be given on amounts owing on stock by soldier settlers, and that there be a revaluation of land. As to the
latter, the government say there will be no revaluation for twenty-five years. It will not be very good news to the struggling soldier settler that there will be no revaluation for twenty-five years, so far as this government is concerned, of the land he is trying to farm on the basis of a valuation which puts success out of his reach. More than that, instead of carrying out the recommendation of the committee as to 60 and 40 per cent, thej' are now offering 40 and 20 per cent, a cut in the first place of one-third of the committee's recommendation and in the second place of one-half. Of all the heartless replies that the government have made to this committee's recommendation the worst is the reply that there will be no revaluation of the land for a period of twenty-five years, thus putting it beyond relief to any of the present settlers on that land. It means that many of them will be forced to leave, will have to give up the unequal struggle and join the exodus that has been going on for the past three or four years to the United States, simply because this government turn a deaf ear not only to their appeals but to the recommendation of the special committee appointed to deal with this very matter, a committee in which, I submit, the government should have confidence. I say this government have failed to do what the country would have them do, failed,I believe, to do what this House of Commons would have them do. The government would be well advised to consider carefully the suggestions made by some hon. members on this side, to withdraw the resolution and replace it by a mor( adequate resolution dealing with the subject: as it should be dealt with by this parliament.

I hope my hon. friend is not
going to attempt to make politics out of this issue. So far it has been comparatively free from that. I pointed out early in the afternoon when t'he resolution was first introduced that the government had before them the report of the Ralston commission. That commission was composed very largely of soldiers. There was no more briLliant soldier in the war than Colonel Ralston himself, and he was sympathetic to the soldiers. The Ralston commission pointed out that the loans had twenty-five years to run and that there was that length of time to establish whether a purchase was a good one or a bad one. I did not say that this government would make no revaluation for twenty-five years. I simply quoted the report of the Ralston commission.

For what purpose
did the minister quote the Ralston commission if it was not to create the impression that there would be no revaluation for twenty-five years?

I quoted the Ralston commission for the information of parliament. I agree with my hon. friend at once that there may be discrimination; that is one of the problems we had before us. A number of these soldier settlers have already paid in full; I think I quoted the figures a while ago. Out of the 500,000 soldiers, roughly speaking, who went to the front, about 24.000 come in under this provision, and the other
475,000	must contribute their share to whatever loss there is by the reduction that we propose under this measure. We must be fair to these men as well as to those who obtained the land.

Does the
minister mean to say that any of them will object?
Possibly some will. I will, for one.

The hon.
member is a politician as well as a Tetumed soldier.
I am a returned soldier first. The hon. gentleman would not say that if he had been in the last parliament.

Does the minister mean
to say it is fair to tax the man who has already paid to help these other men out?

I say that he along with
the rest of us will have to bear his share, and I imagine he will bear it willingly.

Many of these men
have borrowed money for the purpose of paying the government.

I might put on record the
following from the special committee's report:
From a returned soldier point of view, land revaluation would not be warranted, because the soldier settlers under the board who would be affected represent only a portion of the returned soldiers who have gone on the land since the close of the war. The board and the government have been in receipt of many letters from returned soldiers, pointing out that they have had neither cheap money from "the government, freedom from interest, nor any of the advantages that soldier settlers under the board have received. Nevertheless they are returned soldiers who served Canada during the Great War.
What is the object of that quotation?

I had hoped that before this hour the government would have seen fit to withdraw this resolution, reconsider it and put it through the mill again. I hope they will do so yet. In fact, I beg of them, I plead with them, I coax them, I will get down on my knees to them, I will do anything on earth if they will do that.
Come on over here.

This bill is an insult, to use the mildest language I can apply to it, to the returned men who are struggling out on the frontiers of this country trying to make a living. To try and draw an analogy between the soldier settler who has gone out to the frontier sections where most of them are settled with the young fellow who did not see fit to go out and take a part, I do not think is fair. I meet these other fellows who did not become victims of this land settlement scheme, and in saying that I am casting no reflections at all on the late government. I have never done so. I have never doubted their sincerity or honesty in bringing this legislation into effect. I think they introduced it with good motives, but it has been a miserable failure, there is no question about that, and I think it is due to circumstances over which the government probably had no control. I do hope the government will withdraw this measure. I intended to speak at some length to-night, but before going any further I would like to know whether the amendment that has been moved is in order.
