I would like to ask further
whether the government have any idea of withdrawing this resolution and putting it through the mill again, whether they cannot see their way to giving at least some measure of land revaluation.

No, Mr. Chairman. I think
it is better to put through a certain measure of relief such as we are proposing here. I want to say very frankly that I appreciate how my hon. friend from Dauphin feels. I think perhaps if I were representing the constituency that he represents I would take exactly the same attitude. I have had the opportunity of going pretty carefully through these land purchases, and I am bound to admit there is no section in Canada that appeals to me more than a certain section represented by my hon. friend. I think the land up there was not as well purchased as it might have

Soldier Settlement Act
been.. But I think my hon. friend had better allow this to go through as it is, and see what we can work out later on, but I make no commitments as to what will be done.

I am sorry the Acting Minister of Finance has not been in the House all evening. The trend of the speeches this evening has been to urge the government to report progress and reconsider this resolution. I think the government should do it; that is my candid opinion. The minister speaks of the loss that will accrue to the country if there is a revaluation or a remission of interest in connection with these soldier settlement lands, but I would like to ask him if he has considered seriously just what the loss will mean to this country if even fifty per cent of the soldiers abandon their farms and they come back on the government's hands. I doubt if the government would be able to dispose of them as advantageously as the few parcels they have sold. I know in New Brunswick they could not dispose of land to-day for anything like the price they could get two or three years ago, because conditions there during the last four years make it impossible. It is my candid opinion that by revaluation or remission of interest, or whatever other method the government thinks best, you will not make as big a loss as you will by maintaining the present indebtedness and by compelling the soldier settler-I do not like to use the word compel, but that is what it will amount to-to abandon his land and throw it back on the government's hands. The loss in that case will be much greater than anything you would lose by revaluation or remission of interest, and I would again urge the minister to move that the committee rise and report progress in order that this resolution may be reconsidered, and something brought down that will better meet the situation.

In reply to my hon. friend I
cannot do better than repeat the statement which I put on Hansard this afternoon, a record of actual sales of land that we have made:
On page 66 of the report of the committee of last year the board showed that it had resold or accepted offers for 1,672 farms, and the price obtained was $600,000 more than the board had invested.
Since that time the board has resold, mostly to civilians-resident farmers in the country-approximately 50,000 acres of soldier settler lands which have been foreclosed and abandoned by the original settlers. This property cost the board, including the original purchase price plus all permanent improvement advances, $856,000, and it was resold for $895,000 leaving an aggregate gain of approximately $39,000. AM of these sales have been made in the last twelve months, and afford a fairly clear indication of present conditions,
because they cover 46 farms in British Columbia, 72 farms in Alberta, 40 farms in Saskatchewan, 20 farms in Manitoba, 27 farms in Ontario, 14 farms in Quebec,
7 farms in New Brunswick, 9 farms in Nova Scotia, and 4 farms in Prince Edward Island.
In all of the provinces we have been selling these lands for more than they cost.

Would the minister
tell us whether that cost price includes the ten per cent paid by the soldier?

I said this afternoon that
when we are in committee on the bill I will have the chairman of the board here, and will then be able to give the committee all the information it desires.

I think in view of the
fact that this statement has been put on Hansard twice, we should also have on Hansard the amount the soldier settler paid on this land, which I maintain is not included in the figures the minister gave, and they are therefore misleading. They will be broadcasted to the country to-morrow through the press, and I do not think that is fair. The committee got the same statement from the board last year. It sets forth accurately the financial transactions between the board and the soldier settlers, but does not include the ten per cent paid by the soldier, and it therefore is not a real indication of the actual price of -the land when it was bought.

It would represent ninety per
cent of the cost at all events.	-

It might not, because in some cases the soldiers made subsequent payments beyond the ten per cent. I know they did in New Brunswick, as well as making improvements to the farm. Many of these f-arms were later abandoned, and in addi-

The condition of that soldier who leaves without a dollar the farm he has worked on for three or four years, compared with his condition when he received his gratuity on leaving the army of perhaps $600 is one of the saddest features of all. The actual financial standing of the government with respect to the transaction does not bring out the 'whole story.

Is he not better off than the poor soldier who remained in the city and could not get a job? At all events, he has been able to eat and live for three years.

The soldier who stayed in the city had his gratuity with which to maintain himself, and if he sat down and ate it up that was his own lookout. But you cannot compare him with the soldier settler who has been on a farm for three or four years, working fourteen to eighteen hours a day, and who finally has to abandon his farm with possibly a child or two more than when he went on the land, and who leaves the place a little more broken down, a little nearer brokenhearted over the prospect of re-establishing himself. The two cases are not comparable at all because I think the man who went to the city in 1919 and 1920' in most cases got pretty good wages. I think he had a much better show than the man who went to the farm and had to abandon it on account of adverse conditions.
Does my hon. friend know any soldier who works fourteen hours a day who is not able to keep his farm?

Yes, I know them by
the dozen. I would not say he worked fourteen hours every day of the year, but he did it through the rush season and haying and harvesting. No doubt in winter he has some pretty short days, but he works fourteen hours a day on more days than he works less time the year round.

What percentage of the
men have failed to carry on and have given up their farms?

I think I gave that information this afternoon, but I will give my hon. friend some information as to the payments which have been made. The position is that 754 have repaid their entire indebtedness. This year, of the 17,000 settlers with payments due approximately 7,000 have made their payments in full. More than 7,000 others have made substantial payments on account, and altogether approximately 70 per cent of the money due this year has been paid. So that, as I pointed out this afternoon, generally speaking, the soldiers are doing fairly well, and the committee forces me to put upon the record a memorandum. I would rather not have given, because it does not represent, generally speaking, the view of the soldier settler. I repeat he has done fairty well on the whole, although some of them have not done so well. The memorandum reads:
The fact that the board has been able to resell nearly 400.000 acres of abandoned soldier settlement lands, at approximately $700,000 more than its investment in them, and at a time when there has been no active market for farm lands, affords no justification whatever to support a general revaluation of soldier settler lands. It must also be remembered that the great majority of fMr. Power.]
the soldier settler lands which have been abandoned have suffered serious depreciation while in the hands of the settler, and in the period of vacancy subsequent to his abandonment. The board finds generally that the farm which was in a fair state of cultivation at the time it was bought in 1919 or 1920 is run down, weedy, and badly cultivated when thrown up by the soldier settler. In many cases the buildings have actually been wrecked. Cases are not by any means infrequent where the original settler tore up flooring, in barns and stables and even in sections of the house, to use as firewood or for other purposes.
That is not my statement. It is the statement of men who are sympathetic with the soldiers, who are administering the act; but in civil life, as in the army, there are those who have not been the success we hoped they would be, and I repeat again that generally speaking the soldier settlers are doing pretty well, but there are one or two cases throughout the country where I am bound to admit that the soldier was imposed upon by those from whom he purchased, who charged him too much.
One or two cases?

There are a few cases but
the number is very limited. That is the experience of the board who gave their time to the administration of the act.

What percentage have
really thrown up their farms and could be called failures, whether through their fault or the fault of someone else?
The proportion is very small.
May I give the information up to date? A fraction over 20 per cent of the total abandoned their farms at the end of the last fiscal year.
March 31, last.
Yes.

I have been listening to
the debate all day, and I must confess I have not taken much part in it because of the fact that I have heard very little about this matter. Whether I come from a section of the country where the soldier settlers have all been successful or not I do not know. Although on all occasions throughout my experience in the House I have stood up for the rights of the returned soldiers when I could do so, I have yet to receive from a soldier settler in my section of northern Ontario a complaint as to being unable to carry on on his farm. There have been, it is true, not as large a number of soldier settlers in my district as have settled in the prairie provinces, because most of those going on the land prefer the cleared land in the prairie provinces; but where many have taken up land in my section

*-and bukh land at that, where they have to clear the land1-I have not had one write to me and tell me that he has been unable to carry on, and I have a number of settlers in mind. Further I have not had any petition or complaint from any of thpse people or any organization of the soldiers-and I have many of them in my section-claiming remission of their interest, or demanding the cutting down of the valuation or anything of that sort. I must confess frankly that I do not know the reason for it, but the fact remains as I have stated. Perhaps they have all been sucessful.

Might it be because
they thought the government was going to put into effect the recommendation of the committee of last year? That is the case in * New' Brunswick.
Mr. MANIOiN: The soldiers in my district have not been afraid to tell me things; in fact they have been very frank and sometimes even brutal in their statements. I have usually found that the very able and active organizations up in my district have been very ready to fight for the rights of the returned soldiers.
I am pointing this out because I think the Soldier Settlement Act has been abused today more than it deserves to be. I make this statement because anybody listening in the House or in the gallery, or anybody reading Hansard, might draw the conclusion fairly from the remarks which have been made that the soldier settlement legislation has been a complete failure. Certainly, listening to the debate from four o'clock to the present time, one might easily draw that conclusion. I have not drawn any such conclusion, and that is the reason I asked the minister the question,-and the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) gave me the information- as to the number of complete failures. The hon. member told me twenty per cent up to March 31.
I secured the information from Mr. Barnard a few days ago, and I find that there was little over 25 per cent of abandonments up to date, or 5,780 failures.
I discovered the information just after my hon. friend had risen and given the figures. My figures show 23.9 per cent.

I take that to include those who may not necessarily have been failures at all. For example, if a man died and had nobody to whom he could leave the land and nobody to carry on, he would be counted in the 23 per cent?
Yes.
And the minister points out that out of that land that was sold for failure to pay debts and other causes, the government received, I think, $700,000-
The amount was $714,015.85.
More than the mortgages that were against it.
Yes.

So that after all that does not seem to me such a bad record. It is true that when this legislation was put into force valuations were high; nobody disputes that, and I am not arguing against any of the suggestions of my hon. friends that the valuation should be kept down.

In this reckoning has the
expense been accounted for, or is this just a gross statement of what the government have received?

I presume that it is a
gross statement. Of course the minister can answer that better than I can. I am trying to point out the fairly good sides of the whole question, without any particular reason except that I do not like to think that an act which was praised as it was from one end of the world, I might say, to the other, should be looked upon as a failure because twenty or twenty-five per cent of those who went on that land have given it up from one cause or another.
With regard to the treatment of the soldier, the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Black), in that able manner of his which is always for the soldier, pointed out that while the soldiers were treated pretty well, they were not treated too well. I agree entirely with him in that. It would be impossible to treat too well men who offered to give their lives to the country. At the same time we cannot forget that there are limitations beyond which countries or governments .cannot very well go without some danger of wrecking the financial affairs of the country. Therefore, so far as we can, we should endeavour to find out the successes of this act as well as the failures.
When the minister brings in a resolution suggesting, as this resolution does, that forty per cent and twenty per cent be cut off the valuation, that is unfair to the man who has worked day and night and succeeded in making his payments on time. Even the greatest champion of the returned soldier cannot deny that some few of them have been failures through their own fault, and it certainly would appear to me to be rather extraordinary to give a revaluation to such a man who, we will suppose, has been a failure
Soldier Settlement Act

through his own fault, or, in. other words, to hand him back some of the debt which he owes to the country, and on the other hand to give nothing to the other man who has worked hard, been industrious and succeeded in paying his debts. That seems to be a method of rewarding vice and punishing virtue.

Might I just interpose there, that I think the hon. member is rather mistaken in the effect of this resolution? It is true that where a soldier has paid his complete indebtedness and made his payments in advance of the due time, he will not be affected by this legislation, but as long as any indebtedness remains, the amount indicated would be applied to that remaining indebtedness, be it much or little.

I understand that. Of
course, that does not alter the effect of my remarks at all. I think the minister said that 754 had paid up completely. Those 754 soldiers who have paid up completely for their land, because of the fact that they have worked industriously, perhaps put their children and possibly their wives to work as well, because they have accomplished the miraculous, if you will, are to have their virtue in doing so punished. On the other hand, those few who have in some cases at least been more or less worthless-I do not say all by any means; I do not wish to be misunderstood in that, but some have been worthless and the minister gave an indication to show that-are rewarded. In the case I speak of it would1 be unfair. I rose without any desire to take any particular part in the controversy that is going on, but wishing at the same time to impress upon those who want to get as much as they can and, at least, justice for the returned soldier, that it would be wise here to-day to look a little at the advantageous side of the whole matter, at the successes as well as the failures that have occurred. Out of the large number who went on the land, twenty-five per cent under the conditions does not seem to be a heavy percentage of failures. No doubt the valuations were too high. The motion of to-diay to cut down those valuations is, as far as it goes, advantageous to the soldier, and certainly I support it. But we might hesitate to go too repidly in changing the valuations. We should not take too much upon ourselves until the federal government, whichever government it may be, feels that it can see its way clear to go further. At the same time I repeat that I think some arrangement should be made in this resolution to reward those who have been able to pay up their land values in full as well as those who have not been able to do so.

In view of the statement
that the minister has made in regard to lands sold and the profit made on them, it would be well for the minister to tell us the percentage of lands sold or resold from lands that have been salvaged, because in my particular district a number of farms have become vacant as a result of soldiers going away from them, but only one or two have been sold or resold and those that have been resold are the very best farms. The great mass of those which have not been abandoned could not be resold at any price. I understand that nearly
6,000	men have left the farms. At an average of 160 acres apiece, that would mean that we have 1,000,000 acres of land to be resold. So far the minister has stated that we have sold only 400,000 acres of that land, and it is on these 400,000 acres of land that we have had a profit of $700,000. If hon. members will look into this situation they will find that the lands that have been sold are the best lands that could have been sold, and that if we were to sell the other 600,000 acres of land that are still on the hands of the Soldier Settlement Board, we would find that instead of a profit of $700,000, we would have a deficit in excess of that amount. That should go out with the statement that has already gone out.

I will try to produce that
information for my hon. friend when we are in committee on the bill.

There was no option as to when we should begin; the pressure from the returned soldiers, and indeed from the entire 229

An organization to take care of such work is one which it is very difficult to lay down and still more difficult to supervise. The work was evolved of course in the department, the minister having to do mainly with it; but the supervision was largely under Mr. W. J. Black, whose success in choosing his subordinates was really remarkable. It is not needful for me to say now that no political consideration intervened in any part of Canada; nor was any such interference ever charged, I have no doubt at all that the number from one party was about equal to the number from the other so far as the various boards were concerned. The same is true even more emphatically of the province of Manitoba. There excellent work was done by Mr. Peter Wright, of the Council of Agriculture, who assisted us in laying out the whole organization.
Mistakes were made, and I think that perhaps the gravest occurred on the west coast of lake Manitoba. There was a territory opening up for farm settlement into which many pioneers had gone. The land was good and it had belonged to the province; municipalities became organized, and the Manitoba board was induced to settle some soldiers there. In this area is the territory referred to by the hon. member (Mr. Leader) and covered by the letters from the reeves of those municipalities. This district in Manitoba has not been very successful. But I shall not be revealing any secret when I say -that I have myself abandoned six sections up there, and if I had sixty I would abandon them all. The taxes are so high that land simply cannot be held and consequently the district has suffered. I do not know why it has suffered particularly, although I have some conception

of the reason; and the soldiers have suffered with the district. Now, because you argue that 23.9 per cent of the men are not now on the land who originally were there, you do not offer a just criticism against either the scheme or its success. The time will come when there will not be one per cent still, there of those who originally took the land; the time will come when they will all have gone. But that will not prove that the scheme was a total failure, for as the years progress the proportion will be greater and greater; it cannot help but be. The scheme can be judged however by the productive enterprise of those who have gone there, by the homes created and the number of years those homes have survived, and by the government's success in recouping to the treasury a large proportion of the money invested. The whole enterprise has of course encountered the very same difficulties that agriculture in Canada generally has had to meet. Farm lands six years ago were certainly higher in western Canada than they are to-day, just as they were in every other province. And the same is true of stock and equipment. The ordinary farmer therefore has lost money in this country in the last six years. I do not know that the 'hon. member for Victoria and Car-lebon has exaggerated the present situation; but I do not think that his words would fall with much welcome on the ears of the prophets of sunshine who occupy the treasury benches. I noticed an anxious look on the face of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) as he revealed the situation in his own province, and I recalled how I had been castigated when I spoke in language much less pessimistic, being called a prophet of gloom. Now, I never consider it a badge of disloyalty on the part of any man to tell the truth, whatever it may be, and I believe that the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton represented the actual situation. I hope the lesson will fall with good effect upon the ears of hon. gentlemen of the administration.

The right hon. gentleman bewailed the fact that people were leaving the industrial centres while for my part I gave the other side of the picture; they are drifting to the industrial centres from the farms of New Brunswick.

Yes, and to the industrial centres of the United States; and I would rather have them drift to our own industrial centres. I bewailed the fact that they left the industrial centres and that, because they did so, the farmer abandoned the nearby farm. If these things do anything to enlighten hon.

gentlemen to my left, .then the experience even of these bitter years will not have been in vain.
Now I want to say something about the government's plan, which seems to me to be a pretty Slapdash piece of legislation. I do not know upon what principle it is based. Deflation in farm values is as pronounced as deflation in stock values. Of that there can be no question; indeed, stock values are rising somewhat while farm values are not. Real estate is not rising anywhere in Canada; you cannot sell it. But there has been some improvement in stock values as there has also been in grain. Consequently if there is reason for rebating a measure of the price in relation to stock, there is just the same reason for doing so an relation to land. And besides, why should the man who has invested most in stock and least in land be made the special favourite of the government? There are a great many of these men whose whole investment is in land, virtually none in stock; they get nothing at all. But worse than that, the legislation penalizes the best class of soldiers, it penalizes the man who has applied himself the most vigorously and by one means and the other has succeeded in paying off the government-because of his fidelity to his trust and his contract the government throws him to the wind; but the man who is behind, the man who has not paid, the government takes under its wing and says, 'We will help you to pay, ourselves; we will rebate you." Does the government ever expect 'that those 750 odd men who have paid uip in full are going to rest content? Does not the government know that they are going to be right at the doors of the administration in full force? And I do not think they will' likely rest content until they are accorded the same treatment as the government accords those who are in arrear. It is hard enough to deny an ordinary group of citizens something when they can -make out a plausible, even though not a strong case of discrimination, but if they can prove a strong case of discrimination against themselves the government never can and never does deny them. I never knew a government that could furnish an instance-of so doing. All the more is this likely to be so when that group of citizens is a band of soldiers, and they can establish a clear case of discrimination against .themselves; does the government think it can withstand their appeal? It will have to show a lot more stamina and a lot more stability of purpose 'than it has ever shown before.
But that is not the only discrimination. This legislation says: "If a man has not abandoned.

his farm we will relieve him; but if he has, then we will Jet him go." Why do they relieve the man who has not abandoned his farm-why do they relieve anybody? It is on the 'hypothesis that the handicap he was suffering from was too big for him, it was more than he could overcome. Well, what about the fellow who has had to quit altogether, was not his handicap presumably greater still? With respect to the man who is already off the farm the presumption at least is-there will be exceptions-that he suffered some special handicap, his purchase price both of land and chattels owing to deflation in his district was even more than ordinarily great, his discouragement was piled upon him until he had to quit; but because he suffered more than the rest the government lets him go, and' the man who stays on, whose handicaps presumably were not quite so great, the government takes in its lap and feeds at the country's expense. Those discriminations exist, and they cannot be justified.
Would it not be far fairer to treat them all alike and make a general rebate all around? No more than the country could afford, no more than was Considered to be fair, but make it the same for everybody-the same for the cattle man, the same for the farmer man, the same for the fellow that paid, the same for the fellow that abandoned-whatever it is, make it just and equitable, because I warn the government that once they take a certain step with respect to a section, they will not be able to resist those who appeal from other sections on the ground of discrimination. In a word, the standard of rebate they set as respects one lot, that standard they will have to apply to a whole group of men in another lot.

Oh, I see what the hon. member has in his mind. It is on the assumption that we were doing a special favour for some. But the whole act was not based on that in any way whatever. It was based on the wisdom of inviting and encouraging as large a proportion of the returned men as possible to take up farming in Canada, to-build them into the basic foundation industry of the country. Now, those are the objections that appeal to me as against the government's proposal. But I want to say something as to the government's consistency in this whole matter. A year ago the usual plan was followed. A committee of this House was appointed to consider the subject. The committee made an exhaustive inquiry and a report. Then the first thing we heard, the chairman of the-committee was rising in the House and moving the adoption of the report-something that occurred every week last session, at least the last half of the session, something that sometimes occurred daily-the House was asked, without a moment's notice, to declare its opinion on a question of immense magnitude, involving millions of expenditure, and finally to declare its opinion 'on merely one submission. The government accepted the situation, and when that motion was made, the government paid no attention to the protest which I raised. I warned the government of the condition they would get into by that kind of conduct. Indeed, I warned them on several occasions, and other hon. members did so as well. We have in every district

 a local supervisor. In addition we have what is known as a. district supervisor in each -province. I suggested to him -that we ask the Union of Municipalities in, each province to appoint -a third who would be a farmer iof long experience, a -man whose judgment was above question, and who would be made chairman of this revaluation board. The local supervisor knows the situation very well. In each district he knows every road, every settler and the best way to reach that settler, and he can
Soldier Settlement Act

put his finger exactly on ithe spot why that settler has failed. We are paying these men in any case. I am convinced that such a survey could be made of Manitoba in one summer with practically no additional cost except the employment of this chairman. If revaluation does not take place, I am convinced that in another two years we shall have -only about five or ten per cent. The sum of $2,750,000 has already been invested in that one district, and according to the figures secured last year only eighteen per cent has been salvaged from the sales. If this continues as it has in the laslt two years, in another twelve months 'or so we shall have practically lost that amount of $2,750,000.
I should like also to reply to another matter that the minister dealt with in respect to resale of farms. I know the minister is sincere and honest, but I am sure if he had been in possession of the real facts, he would never have made those statements at all. There is an odd good farm here and there in the district, and it is only farms of this kind that are sold. The minister gave us the number of these resales in the last year and they were .about one-fifth of the number of abandonments; which proves .that it is only the odd good farms that are sold. In my own district the few farms that have been sold are just as likely to revert to the government; in fact I think they are more likely to do so. The fact that there is a change in tenants does not assure success.
I a,m sorry to prolong this debate, but I do not think the minister should persist in refusing to withdraw this motion and to reconsider the matter. I again impress upon him that a physical revaluation of the * land is not the problem which be thinks it is. It is a very simple thing and it would be to the advantage of .the government to have this done.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Surely the
hon. member would not suggest that there should be a reduction in the investment to the extent of 75 per cent.

Absolutely. I have proven
that in my own district-and the same is true throughout the whole Dominion-only 18 per cent was salvaged in the resales. Let me give the result of one sale I attended before leaving for Ottawa. In this case stock and equipment that were valued at $2,500 brought $375.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This may
be true in one or two districts; it may be true in the hon. member's particular locality.

And for that reason it is difficult to accept the suggestion made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), because you cannot approach the matter from that standpoint. But if we are required to make a 75 per cent reduction all round we might as well abandon the whole thing.

If we continue as we are
doing now the situation will be still worse. We have been able to salvage only 18 per cent from the sale of chattels, and I can assure the minister that he will find in the lake Manitoba section that the lands have not resold for 25 per cent of their original cost. The only salvation for the settlers in such districts is to bring about a physical revaluation, and I have endeavoured to point out how this can be done at a minimum cost, and indeed at practically no cost at all.
There is invested in my constituency about $2,750,000, and we had already lost a year ago $600,000 of that. To-day we can easily add $400,000 to this loss, bringing the total up to about $1,000,000. We are therefore losing in any case. In the municipality of Lawrence, which is in the very heart of the lake Manitoba section, of sixteen schools last fall only four were open. I believe the province has adopted a very progressive policy in the matter of education and has now opened nearly all these schools; nevertheless the reason why all these schools were closed was that the soldiers had moved away leaving no one to maintain them. In districts where before there were between twenty and twenty-five families there are now left only four or five families to carry on; and the burden is becoming more and more oppressive. The situation is so serious in this particular municipality that it has got into the hands of the receiver; and there is a large section between that and the lake which is unorganized and is in a most deplorable condition. I think it was the hon. member to my right (Mr. Manion) who referred to men who had succeeded here and there. Well, in some sections you will find they have succeeded to the extent of 90 or 100 per cent; but when you go into Selkirk, Neepawa and1 Dauphin you find that they have failed almost 100 per cent. The reason is that the potential value is not there; it was not in the farms in the first instance. The minister himself admitted a few minutes ago that the Dauphin section became the victim of inflation to an extent that did not exist in any other part of the Dominion, and this is due to the fact that this was the first section to be settled; it was here that the first application was made.

Northwest Territories Act
A number of more or less unscruplous land companies owning large tracts of land got the ear of the inspectors and were able to unload upon them at handsome prices large sections which were in turn unloaded on the soldiers. Many of these parcels are still held by the soldiers, and I contend again that there is only one hope for these men. Let us write them all and say, "For God's sake get out of there and go where you can make a living"; or else let us do something practical in their behalf. I once more implore the minister to reconsider this matter to see whether we cannot find a means of helping the soldiers in the way I have suggested.

When the report of the committee was submitted last year it was pointed out that the country would sustain a loss of some $38,000,000 under this scheme; and as I pointed out this afternoon we have made remissions to the soldiers amounting to approximately $12,000,000. This afternoon we submitted to the House a resolution based upon which the government would bring in a bill to provide as a further rebate:
Forty per centum of the purchase price of all live stock advanced to the settler and purchased prior to the first day of October, 1920;
Twenty per centum of the purchase price of all live stock advanced to the settler and purchased on or after the first day of October, 1920, and prior to the first day of October, 1921.
We have been considering this resolution all day and it is now approaching midnight, and as we have had some of the officials here in readiness to go on with supply, I move that the committee rise and report progress and ask leave to sit again.

When the minister
takes this matter up again will he inform the committee how much has been paid in full on the farms under the 10 per cent initial payment; how much has been salvaged; what the total collections have been in the past year-and the cost of administration.

I shall take a note of the
questions.
Progress reported.
